title: Interactive Data Apps with Streamlit
subtitle: Turn Python analysis into interactive web apps: widgets, layouts, charts, caching, session state, forms and multipage navigation, tested with AppTest and ready to deploy.
outcomes: Explain Streamlit's rerun model, and build apps from text and data elements and widgets
Lay out apps with the sidebar, columns and tabs, and show data with charts, configured tables, metrics and downloads
Speed apps up with st.cache_data, st.cache_resource and fragments, choosing the right one for each job
Keep state across reruns with session state, callbacks and forms, and store shared data in a database
Build multipage apps with st.navigation, test them with AppTest and pytest, and prepare them for deployment
prerequisites: Python and pandas: functions, modules, DataFrames, filtering and grouping, as in Data Analysis with Python and pandas. Data Visualisation with Matplotlib, Seaborn and Plotly helps with the charts. You need Python 3.10 or later; the course installs streamlit and pytest in a virtual environment and makes its data with a script. Docker and a GitHub account are optional, for deployment.
description:
Streamlit turns a Python script into a web app: add a slider and a chart, and anyone with a browser can explore your analysis. This course takes you from a first script to a tested, multipage app ready to deploy, building one app all the way through: an explorer of daily air-quality readings from four (made-up) monitoring stations. You'll start with how Streamlit works, rerunning the whole script on every interaction, and build the first version from text, widgets, metrics and a chart. Then you'll lay it out with a sidebar, columns and tabs, draw Altair charts with threshold lines, format tables with column_config and offer the filtered data as a download.

Next come the parts that make real apps work: caching data with st.cache_data and sharing a database connection with st.cache_resource, rerunning only part of a page with fragments, keeping values in session state, changing them safely with callbacks, and collecting community reports with a validated form stored in SQLite. Finally you'll split the app into pages with st.navigation, test every page with Streamlit's AppTest and pytest, smoke-test the server's health endpoint, and prepare deployment with a theme, secrets, requirements and a Dockerfile, or Streamlit Community Cloud. Every lab is checked by tests that run without a browser, and the capstone is a deployed data app of your own. It builds on Data Analysis with Python and pandas; AI-Powered Business Intelligence Fundamentals and Data Storytelling and Dashboard Design are good companions.

modules.title: Streamlit basics: scripts, elements and widgets
modules.summary: See how Streamlit turns a Python script into a web app that reruns on every interaction, then build a first data app from text, data elements and widgets, and test it with AppTest.

lessons.title: How a Streamlit app runs
objectives: Run a Streamlit app and explain the rerun model
Display text and data with st.write, magic and the text elements
Run an app without a browser, for servers and tests
key_points: streamlit run app.py starts a local web server, by default at http://localhost:8501, and opens the app in a browser; the app is an ordinary Python script, and Ctrl+C in the terminal stops the server.

Streamlit reruns the whole script from top to bottom every time a user changes a widget, with the widget's new value; this rerun model is why slow steps need caching and why values that must survive need session state.

st.write displays almost anything (text, numbers, DataFrames, charts), and 'magic' shows a variable or expression written alone on a line as if it were passed to st.write; st.title, st.header, st.markdown and st.caption format text.
When you save the script, the app offers Rerun and Always rerun; pressing R in the app reruns it, and errors appear in the page with their traceback, so the edit, save and look loop is quick.

streamlit run app.py --server.headless true starts the server without opening a browser, for servers and smoke tests; --server.port changes the port, and the same settings can live in .streamlit/config.toml.

walkthrough.title: Install Streamlit and run your first app

steps.do: Make a folder for the course with its own virtual environment and activate it. On Windows, create it with py -m venv .venv and activate it with .venv\Scripts\activate.

cd streamlit-course
python3 -m venv .venv
source .venv/bin/activate

steps.do: Run Streamlit's built-in demo app.
steps.code: streamlit hello
steps.see: A browser tab opens at http://localhost:8501 with demos to explore.

steps.do: Stop the server in the terminal.
Save this as hello_app.py: a title, some Markdown, a widget and magic.
steps.code:
import streamlit as st

st.title("Hello, Streamlit")
name = st.text_input("Your name", "world")
st.markdown(f"Hello, **{name}**!")
len(name)  # magic: shown as if passed to st.write

steps.do: Run it, type a name and press Enter: the whole script reruns and the greeting and the number change.
steps.code: streamlit run hello_app.py

Stop it, then run it headless and check the health endpoint from a second terminal.
steps.code:
streamlit run hello_app.py --server.headless true
# in a second terminal:
curl -s -w " HTTP %{http_code}\n" http://localhost:8501/_stcore/health

lessons.title: Widgets: input that reruns the app
objectives: Add sliders, select boxes, multiselects, dates, numbers and text inputs, and use the values they return
Explain why st.button is True for one run only
Handle a date range that is still being chosen
key_points: Each widget call draws the widget and returns its current value: st.slider returns a number (or a tuple for a range), st.selectbox one option, st.multiselect a list, st.checkbox and st.toggle True or False, and st.text_input a string.
Give widgets sensible defaults (value=, default=, index=) and help= text, and limit choices (min_value, max_value, options) so users can't enter values the app can't handle.
st.date_input with a tuple of two dates lets users pick a range, and returns a tuple; while only the first date has been picked, the tuple has one date, so check len(dates) == 2 before using it.
st.button returns True only on the rerun its click causes, and False on every later run, so anything that must be remembered after a click has to be stored in session state.
st.number_input returns an int or a float to match its arguments: value=0 gives whole numbers and value=0.0 decimals, so mixing the two raises an error.

lessons.title: Widget identity, keys and showing results
objectives: Give widgets keys and avoid duplicate-widget errors
Show results with metrics, tables, charts and status messages
Stop a run early with st.stop when input is missing
key_points: Streamlit tells widgets apart by their parameters, so two identical widgets without key= raise a duplicate element error; key= gives a widget a unique name, which is also its key in st.session_state.
st.metric(label, value, delta) shows a headline number with an optional change; delta_color='inverse' colours a fall green, for measures where lower is better, such as pollution.

st.dataframe shows an interactive table that users can sort, resize and search, st.table a static one, and st.line_chart(df, x='date', y='pm25', color='station') a quick chart straight from long data.
st.success, st.info, st.warning and st.error show status messages, and st.stop() ends the run at that point, which is the clean way to wait for missing input, such as no stations chosen.
Keep calculations in plain functions in a separate module, such as aq.py, and keep the app script for layout and widgets: the functions can then be tested, and reused, without Streamlit.

"""Write air_quality.csv: daily readings from four made-up monitoring stations, January to April 2026.

Uses only the standard library, and random.random() with a fixed seed, so every computer makes the same file.
"""
import csv
import random
from datetime import date, timedelta

random.seed(2026)
STATIONS = [("Harbour", 14.0, 31.0), ("Old Town", 12.5, 38.0), ("Riverside", 9.0, 22.0), ("Hillcrest", 6.5, 14.0)]
start, days = date(2026, 1, 1), 120


def noise():
    """A number between -1 and 1, most often near 0."""
    return (random.random() + random.random() + random.random() - 1.5) / 1.5


rows = []
for i in range(days):
    day = start + timedelta(days=i)
    season = 1.25 - 0.4 * i / (days - 1)                     # winter air is dirtier
    episode = 2.2 if date(2026, 2, 10) <= day <= date(2026, 2, 14) else 1.0   # a five-day smog episode
    traffic = {5: 0.85, 6: 0.75}.get(day.weekday(), 1.1)      # less traffic at weekends
    for name, pm25, no2 in STATIONS:
        rows.append([day.isoformat(), name, round(pm25 * season * episode * (1 + 0.25 * noise()), 1),
                     round(no2 * traffic * (1 + 0.2 * noise()), 1)])

with open("air_quality.csv", "w", newline="", encoding="utf-8") as f:
    writer = csv.writer(f)
    writer.writerow(["date", "station", "pm25", "no2"])
    writer.writerows(rows)
print(f"Wrote air_quality.csv: {len(rows)} rows, {len(STATIONS)} stations, {rows[0][0]} to {rows[-1][0]}")

"""Tests for the air quality app. Run them with:  python -m pytest -q"""
from streamlit.testing.v1 import AppTest

import aq


def test_helpers():
    df = aq.load_readings()
    assert len(df) == 480
    march = aq.filter_readings(df, ["Harbour"], "2026-03-01", "2026-03-31")
    assert len(march) == 31
    assert aq.days_above(march, 15) == 5


def test_app_defaults():
    at = AppTest.from_file("app.py").run(timeout=10)
    assert not at.exception
    assert at.title[0].value == "Air quality explorer"
    assert at.metric[0].value == "11.5 µg/m³"
    assert at.metric[1].value == "77"


def test_threshold_slider():
    at = AppTest.from_file("app.py").run(timeout=10)
    at.slider[0].set_value(30).run()
    assert at.metric[1].value == "6"


def test_no_stations_warns():
    at = AppTest.from_file("app.py").run(timeout=10)
    at.multiselect[0].set_value([]).run()
    assert at.warning[0].value == "Choose at least one station."

hints: ValueError: not enough values to unpack means dates had one date: the validate block's len(dates) check must come before filter_readings(df, stations, *dates).
FileNotFoundError: air_quality.csv means make_data.py hasn't been run in this folder, or the app was started from another folder.
If a test fails on a metric, run the app and compare its value with the test's: the tests expect the data that make_data.py writes, unchanged.
Port 8501 already in use? Stop the other Streamlit app, or add --server.port 8502 (and use 8502 in the curl command).
RuntimeError: AppTest script run timed out means a run took longer than its timeout, which can happen on a busy or slow computer: raise it, as in run(timeout=20).

modules.title: Layout, charts and data display
modules.summary: Arrange an app with the sidebar, columns, tabs and containers, choose between Streamlit's built-in charts and Altair, Plotly or Matplotlib, and present data with configured tables, metrics and downloads.

lessons.title: Layout: sidebar, columns, tabs and containers
objectives: Configure the page and move controls into the sidebar
Arrange content with columns, tabs, expanders and containers
Update a placeholder in place with st.empty
key_points: st.set_page_config(page_title=..., page_icon=..., layout='wide') sets the browser tab's title and icon and lets content use the full width; recent versions allow calling it more than once, while older ones required it to be the first Streamlit command.
Anything written inside with st.sidebar: (or with st.sidebar.slider and similar) goes in the collapsible sidebar, the usual place for filters, so the main area is left for results.

st.columns(3) or st.columns([2, 1]) returns columns to write into side by side, with gap= and vertical_alignment= to adjust them; st.tabs(['Trend', 'Data']) returns tabs, and every tab's code runs on every rerun, whichever tab is showing.
st.expander hides detail until it's opened, st.container(border=True) groups elements (height= makes it scroll), and st.popover opens a small panel from a button.
st.empty() reserves a slot that later calls replace, such as a status line updated in a loop; each write to the placeholder overwrites what was there.

lessons.title: Charts: built-in, Altair, Plotly and Matplotlib
objectives: Use Streamlit's built-in charts for quick views of long or wide data
Show Altair, Plotly and Matplotlib figures in an app
Size charts and react to selections
key_points: st.line_chart, st.bar_chart, st.area_chart and st.scatter_chart draw straight from a DataFrame: x= and y= name the columns and color= splits long data into series; they're quick, but offer few options.
st.altair_chart shows an Altair (Vega-Lite) chart, which can layer marks, such as a line plus a dashed threshold rule, and add tooltips; Streamlit applies its own theme unless theme=None is passed.
st.plotly_chart shows an interactive Plotly figure, and st.pyplot(fig) a Matplotlib one: pass the figure object you created rather than relying on pyplot's current figure.
Charts fill the width of their container by default; in recent versions width= and height= set their size, and use_container_width is deprecated.
Altair and Plotly charts, and st.dataframe, can return what the user selects: on_select='rerun' reruns the app with the selection, so one chart can filter another.

lessons.title: Tables, metrics and downloads
objectives: Format tables with column_config
Let users edit data with st.data_editor
Offer filtered data as a download
key_points: column_config tells st.dataframe how to show each column: st.column_config.NumberColumn('PM2.5', format='%.1f'), DateColumn(format='D MMM YYYY'), ProgressColumn for values in a range and LineChartColumn for a small chart in each cell; hide_index=True hides the index.
st.data_editor shows an editable table and returns the edited DataFrame; num_rows='dynamic' lets users add and delete rows, and disabled= locks columns that shouldn't change.
st.metric(label, value, delta) puts a headline figure over its change; three metrics in st.columns(3) make a row of KPI tiles, and border=True draws a box round each.

st.download_button('Download CSV', df.to_csv(index=False), file_name='readings.csv', mime='text/csv') lets users save exactly what they're looking at; clicking it reruns the app unless on_click='ignore' is set, in recent versions.
Show units in the column names or formats, round to a sensible precision and put the most useful columns first (column_order=), so a table reads as clearly as a chart.

lab.title: Lay out the explorer with tabs, charts and a download
lab.goal: Turn the first version into a wide, organised app: filters in the sidebar, a row of three metrics with a delta, and tabs holding an Altair chart with a threshold line, a station summary with a bar chart and formatted table, and the filtered data with a download button.
setup: The course folder and virtual environment from the module 1 lab
The starter files: app.py (with TODOs), aq.py, test_app.py and make_data.py; run python make_data.py first if air_quality.csv isn't in the folder

steps.do: Replace the page-config TODO at the top of app.py, so the app uses the full width.
steps.code: st.set_page_config(page_title="Air quality explorer", page_icon="🌫️", layout="wide")

steps.do: Replace the sidebar TODO: the three filters, under a header, in the sidebar.
steps.code:
with st.sidebar:
    st.header("Filters")
    stations = st.multiselect("Stations", aq.STATIONS, default=aq.STATIONS)
    threshold = st.slider("PM2.5 threshold (µg/m³)", 5, 50, aq.GUIDELINE_PM25)
    dates = st.date_input("Dates", value=(first, last), min_value=first, max_value=last)

steps.do: Replace the metrics TODO: three metrics in columns, the first with its change on the whole period (inverse colours, because lower is better).
steps.code:
whole = aq.filter_readings(df, stations, first, last)
change = view["pm25"].mean() - whole["pm25"].mean()
col1, col2, col3 = st.columns(3)
col1.metric("Mean PM2.5", f"{view['pm25'].mean():.1f} µg/m³", delta=f"{change:+.1f} on the whole period",
            delta_color="inverse")
col2.metric("Highest daily PM2.5", f"{view['pm25'].max():.1f} µg/m³")
col3.metric("Readings above the threshold", aq.days_above(view, threshold))

steps.do: Replace the tabs TODO: a layered Altair chart, a station summary with a horizontal bar chart and a configured table, and the data with a download button.
steps.code:
trend, by_station, data = st.tabs(["Trend", "Stations", "Data"])
with trend:
    line = alt.Chart(view).mark_line().encode(
        x=alt.X("date:T", title=None), y=alt.Y("pm25:Q", title="PM2.5 (µg/m³)"),
        color=alt.Color("station:N", title="Station"), tooltip=["date:T", "station:N", "pm25:Q", "no2:Q"])
    rule = alt.Chart(pd.DataFrame({"threshold": [threshold]})).mark_rule(strokeDash=[4, 4]).encode(y="threshold:Q")
    st.altair_chart(line + rule)
with by_station:
    summary = aq.summarise(view, threshold)
    st.bar_chart(summary["above"], horizontal=True, x_label="Readings above the threshold", y_label="")
    st.dataframe(summary, column_config={
        "mean_pm25": st.column_config.NumberColumn("Mean PM2.5", format="%.1f µg/m³"),
        "max_pm25": st.column_config.NumberColumn("Highest PM2.5", format="%.1f µg/m³"),
        "above": st.column_config.ProgressColumn("Above threshold", min_value=0, max_value=len(view["date"].unique()),
                                                  format="%d"),
        "mean_no2": st.column_config.NumberColumn("Mean NO₂", format="%.1f µg/m³")})
with data:
    st.dataframe(view, hide_index=True, column_config={
        "date": st.column_config.DateColumn("Date", format="D MMM YYYY"),
        "pm25": st.column_config.NumberColumn("PM2.5 (µg/m³)", format="%.1f"),
        "no2": st.column_config.NumberColumn("NO₂ (µg/m³)", format="%.1f")})
    st.download_button("Download these readings (CSV)", view.to_csv(index=False),
                       file_name="air_quality_filtered.csv", mime="text/csv")

steps.code: streamlit run app.py
steps.see: Mean PM2.5 13.9 µg/m³, with +2.4 on the whole period shown in red because lower is better.

steps.see: A file called air_quality_filtered.csv in your downloads.

steps.do: Run the tests.
steps.code: python -m pytest -q
steps.see: 4 passed

The download gives the filtered readings.

modules.title: Caching and performance
modules.summary: Stop the rerun model from repeating slow work: cache data with st.cache_data, share connections and models with st.cache_resource, and rerun only part of an app with fragments.

lessons.title: Caching data with st.cache_data
objectives: Cache the results of slow functions with st.cache_data
Control a cache's lifetime and size
Explain how arguments are hashed and why callers get copies
key_points: @st.cache_data stores a function's return value, keyed by its arguments and its code: the first call runs the function, and later calls with the same arguments, in any session, return the stored result without running it.

Each call returns a copy of the cached value (it's stored pickled), so changing the returned DataFrame can't corrupt the cache; the value must therefore be picklable, such as a DataFrame, a list or a string.
ttl='1h' (or seconds, or a timedelta) makes entries expire so fresh data is fetched, max_entries= caps how many argument combinations are kept, and show_spinner= sets the message shown while it runs.
Arguments must be hashable for the cache key; a parameter whose name starts with an underscore, such as _conn, is left out of the key, for objects like connections that can't be hashed.
load.clear() empties one function's cache and st.cache_data.clear() every data cache; the app's menu and the C key also clear caches while you develop.
st.cache was removed: use st.cache_data for data and st.cache_resource for shared objects.

lessons.title: Sharing resources with st.cache_resource
objectives: Share one database connection or model across every session with st.cache_resource
Choose between st.cache_data and st.cache_resource
Avoid the thread-safety and mutation traps of shared objects
key_points: @st.cache_resource runs a function once and returns the same object to every later call, from every session, without copying it: the right tool for database connections, HTTP clients and machine learning models.

Use cache_data for data you compute or download, which should be copied for each caller, and cache_resource for objects that can't be pickled or that should exist only once, such as a model too large to load per user.

A shared object is used from several sessions' threads at once, so it must be thread-safe and must not be changed for one user: sqlite3.connect needs check_same_thread=False to be shared, and per-user values belong in session state.
cache_resource also takes ttl= and max_entries=, and validate= can check that a cached object is still usable, such as a connection that may have dropped, before it's returned.
Clearing a resource cache (get_db.clear() or st.cache_resource.clear()) makes the next call create a new object, which tests use to start from a clean state.

lessons.title: Fragments and other speed-ups
objectives: Rerun part of an app with st.fragment
Refresh part of an app on a timer
Find slow steps and give users feedback while they run
key_points: @st.fragment turns a function into a fragment: when a widget inside it changes, only the fragment reruns, not the whole script, which keeps a busy page responsive.
run_every='10s' reruns a fragment on a timer, for a live panel such as the latest readings, and st.rerun(scope='fragment') reruns just the fragment from inside it.
Fragments can't be used to skip work that the rest of the script needs; values that other parts of the app use must still be stored in session state or recomputed there.
Measure before optimising: time.perf_counter() around a step, or the time shown in a status message, shows which step is slow; filter data early and draw fewer points rather than plotting every row.
st.spinner('Loading...') shows a message while a block runs, and st.status shows a collapsible box of progress steps, so users know the app is working.

"""Write air_quality.csv: daily readings from four made-up monitoring stations, January to April 2026.

Uses only the standard library, and random.random() with a fixed seed, so every computer makes the same file.
"""
import csv
import random
from datetime import date, timedelta

random.seed(2026)
STATIONS = [("Harbour", 14.0, 31.0), ("Old Town", 12.5, 38.0), ("Riverside", 9.0, 22.0), ("Hillcrest", 6.5, 14.0)]
start, days = date(2026, 1, 1), 120


def noise():
    """A number between -1 and 1, most often near 0."""
    return (random.random() + random.random() + random.random() - 1.5) / 1.5


rows = []
for i in range(days):
    day = start + timedelta(days=i)
    season = 1.25 - 0.4 * i / (days - 1)                     # winter air is dirtier
    episode = 2.2 if date(2026, 2, 10) <= day <= date(2026, 2, 14) else 1.0   # a five-day smog episode
    traffic = {5: 0.85, 6: 0.75}.get(day.weekday(), 1.1)      # less traffic at weekends
    for name, pm25, no2 in STATIONS:
        rows.append([day.isoformat(), name, round(pm25 * season * episode * (1 + 0.25 * noise()), 1),
                     round(no2 * traffic * (1 + 0.2 * noise()), 1)])

with open("air_quality.csv", "w", newline="", encoding="utf-8") as f:
    writer = csv.writer(f)
    writer.writerow(["date", "station", "pm25", "no2"])
    writer.writerows(rows)
print(f"Wrote air_quality.csv: {len(rows)} rows, {len(STATIONS)} stations, {rows[0][0]} to {rows[-1][0]}")

modules.title: Session state, callbacks and forms
modules.summary: Keep values across reruns with session state, change state safely with callbacks, and collect input with forms that submit in one go and store their results in a database.

lessons.title: Session state
objectives: Store values across reruns with st.session_state
Initialise state safely and link widgets to it with keys
Explain what a session is and when state is lost
key_points: st.session_state is a dictionary-like store that survives reruns for one session: st.session_state.count and st.session_state['count'] both work, and values can be any Python object.
Initialise each value once, before it's used: if 'count' not in st.session_state: st.session_state.count = 0, or st.session_state.setdefault('count', 0).
A session is one browser tab connected to the app: each user, and each tab, has its own state, and reloading the page starts a new session with empty state.
A widget with key='threshold' keeps its value in st.session_state.threshold, so other code can read it, and setting that key before the widget is drawn sets the widget's value.

Set a widget's starting value either with its value or default argument or through session state, not both: Streamlit warns when a widget has a default and its key was also set through the Session State API.

lessons.title: Callbacks and changing state safely
objectives: Use on_change and on_click callbacks to update state
Reset widgets from a callback
Avoid changing a widget's state after it's drawn
key_points: on_click= (buttons) and on_change= (other widgets) name a function that runs before the script reruns; args= and kwargs= pass it arguments, as in st.button('Add', on_click=add, args=(5,)).
Because a callback runs before any widget is drawn, it may set widgets' values: a 'Reset filters' button whose callback sets st.session_state.threshold = 15 moves the slider back on the next run.
Assigning to a widget's key after the widget has been drawn in the same run raises an error (StreamlitWidgetAlreadyInstantiatedError in recent versions): do it in a callback, or before the widget.
Without callbacks, a button's effect appears one run late, because the code that reads the state runs before the button's own block; callbacks avoid that ordering problem.
st.rerun() reruns the script immediately, for example after changing state that earlier parts of the page have already used; use it sparingly, because it can loop.

lessons.title: Forms and dialogs
objectives: Batch inputs into a form that submits in one go
Validate a form's input and give feedback
Know the rules forms impose, and when a dialog fits better
key_points: with st.form('report'): groups widgets so that changing them doesn't rerun the app; everything is sent together when st.form_submit_button is clicked, which returns True on that run.
clear_on_submit=True resets the form's widgets after submission, and each form needs a unique key; forms can't be nested, and an ordinary st.button can't be placed inside one.

Only the submit button may have a callback, and the other widgets' values are only up to date after submission, so validate after the submit: check the values, then show st.error or save and show st.success.
Store each submission where it needs to live: st.session_state for this user's session only, or a database (through a connection cached with st.cache_resource) for data every user should see.
@st.dialog('Title') turns a function into a modal dialog that opens when it's called, for a short focused task such as confirming a deletion; st.toast shows a brief notification in the corner.

"""Air quality helpers: plain functions, so they can be tested without Streamlit."""
import pandas as pd

STATIONS = ["Harbour", "Old Town", "Riverside", "Hillcrest"]
GUIDELINE_PM25 = 15  # µg/m³ as a 24-hour mean: the WHO's 2021 air quality guideline


def load_readings(path="air_quality.csv"):
    """Read the daily readings, with dates as datetimes."""
    return pd.read_csv(path, parse_dates=["date"])


def filter_readings(df, stations, start, end):
    """Readings for the chosen stations between two dates, both included."""
    keep = df["station"].isin(stations) & df["date"].between(pd.Timestamp(start), pd.Timestamp(end))
    return df.loc[keep]


def days_above(df, threshold):
    """How many daily readings are above the threshold."""
    return int((df["pm25"] > threshold).sum())


def summarise(df, threshold=GUIDELINE_PM25):
    """One row per station: mean and highest PM2.5, readings above the threshold, and mean NO2."""
    out = df.groupby("station").agg(mean_pm25=("pm25", "mean"), max_pm25=("pm25", "max"),
                                    above=("pm25", lambda s: int((s > threshold).sum())),
                                    mean_no2=("no2", "mean"))
    return out.round(1).sort_values("mean_pm25", ascending=False)


import os
import sqlite3

LOADS = 0          # how many times the CSV has been read, so tests can check the cache
CONNECTIONS = 0    # how many database connections have been opened


def load_readings_counted(path="air_quality.csv"):
    """load_readings, counting each call."""
    global LOADS
    LOADS += 1
    return load_readings(path)


def connect(path=None):
    """Open the reports database, creating its table if needed. The AQ_DB variable overrides the file name."""
    global CONNECTIONS
    CONNECTIONS += 1
    conn = sqlite3.connect(path or os.environ.get("AQ_DB", "reports.db"), check_same_thread=False)
    conn.execute("CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS reports (station TEXT, day TEXT, pm25 REAL, note TEXT)")
    return conn


def count_reports(conn):
    return conn.execute("SELECT COUNT(*) FROM reports").fetchone()[0]

modules.title: Multipage apps, testing and deployment
modules.summary: Split the app into pages with st.navigation and shared filters, test every page with AppTest, and deploy it with its configuration and secrets to Streamlit Community Cloud or a Docker container.

lessons.title: Multipage apps with st.navigation
objectives: Define pages with st.Page and a menu with st.navigation
Share filters and data between pages
Link and switch between pages
key_points: st.Page('app_pages/report.py', title='Report a reading', icon=':material/edit_note:') defines a page from a file (or a function); st.navigation(pages) builds the menu and returns the current page, which the entrypoint must run with page.run().
Passing a dictionary, such as {'Explore': [...], 'Contribute': [...]}, groups pages into sections, and position='top' moves the menu from the sidebar to the top of the page.
The entrypoint file runs on every page, so widgets drawn there, such as sidebar filters with keys, appear on every page and keep their values; pages read them from st.session_state.
Put cached loaders in a shared module, such as data.py, that every page imports, so all pages use one cache and one database connection.

st.page_link draws a link to another page and st.switch_page('app_pages/report.py') jumps to one in code; once st.navigation runs, Streamlit ignores the older pages/ folder convention, so name the page folder something else, such as app_pages.

lessons.title: Testing Streamlit apps
objectives: Unit-test an app's logic by importing it
Test the app itself with AppTest: run it, change widgets and check what it shows
Smoke-test a running app with its health endpoint
key_points: Logic in plain functions, such as aq.summarise, is tested like any Python code: import it in a pytest file and assert on the result, with no Streamlit involved.

from streamlit.testing.v1 import AppTest; at = AppTest.from_file('app.py').run() runs the script without a browser; at.title, at.metric, at.warning and other lists hold what it drew, and at.exception holds any error.

Widgets are driven like a user would: at.slider[0].set_value(30).run(), at.button[0].click().run(), at.sidebar.multiselect[0].set_value([]).run(); at.session_state and at.switch_page('app_pages/x.py') cover state and pages.

AppTest's run has a timeout (3 seconds by default; run(timeout=10) allows more), and caches persist between tests in one process, so clear them with st.cache_data.clear() or st.cache_resource.clear() when a test needs a clean start.
Before deploying, run the real server headless and request /_stcore/health, which answers ok when the server is up; container platforms use the same endpoint for health checks.

lessons.title: Deploying: configuration, secrets and hosting
objectives: Configure an app with config.toml and pin its requirements
Keep secrets out of the code with secrets.toml and st.secrets
Deploy to Streamlit Community Cloud or run in Docker
key_points: .streamlit/config.toml holds settings such as [theme] base = 'light' and primaryColor, and [server] port and headless; command-line flags override it, and streamlit config show lists every option.

Secrets go in .streamlit/secrets.toml locally, read as st.secrets['db']['password'], and never in the repository: add the file to .gitignore and enter the same TOML in the hosting platform's secrets settings instead.
requirements.txt lists the packages to install, with minimum or exact versions, so the deployed app gets the same libraries you tested with.

Streamlit Community Cloud deploys an app from a GitHub repository: choose the repository, branch and entrypoint file, set the Python version and secrets in the advanced settings, and the app is served at a streamlit.app address and redeploys when you push.
In Docker, install the requirements, expose port 8501 and run streamlit run with --server.address=0.0.0.0 so the server is reachable from outside the container, with a HEALTHCHECK on /_stcore/health.

Apps are public unless you restrict them: recent versions add st.login for sign-in with an OpenID Connect provider, configured under [auth] in secrets.toml, or the app can sit behind your organisation's own sign-in.

"""Write air_quality.csv: daily readings from four made-up monitoring stations, January to April 2026.

Uses only the standard library, and random.random() with a fixed seed, so every computer makes the same file.
"""
import csv
import random
from datetime import date, timedelta

random.seed(2026)
STATIONS = [("Harbour", 14.0, 31.0), ("Old Town", 12.5, 38.0), ("Riverside", 9.0, 22.0), ("Hillcrest", 6.5, 14.0)]
start, days = date(2026, 1, 1), 120


def noise():
    """A number between -1 and 1, most often near 0."""
    return (random.random() + random.random() + random.random() - 1.5) / 1.5


rows = []
for i in range(days):
    day = start + timedelta(days=i)
    season = 1.25 - 0.4 * i / (days - 1)                     # winter air is dirtier
    episode = 2.2 if date(2026, 2, 10) <= day <= date(2026, 2, 14) else 1.0   # a five-day smog episode
    traffic = {5: 0.85, 6: 0.75}.get(day.weekday(), 1.1)      # less traffic at weekends
    for name, pm25, no2 in STATIONS:
        rows.append([day.isoformat(), name, round(pm25 * season * episode * (1 + 0.25 * noise()), 1),
                     round(no2 * traffic * (1 + 0.2 * noise()), 1)])

with open("air_quality.csv", "w", newline="", encoding="utf-8") as f:
    writer = csv.writer(f)
    writer.writerow(["date", "station", "pm25", "no2"])
    writer.writerows(rows)
print(f"Wrote air_quality.csv: {len(rows)} rows, {len(STATIONS)} stations, {rows[0][0]} to {rows[-1][0]}")

import altair as alt

import aq

"""Report page: a form that stores community readings in the shared database."""
import streamlit as st

import aq
import data

st.title("Report a reading")
db = data.db()
with st.form("report", clear_on_submit=True):
    station = st.selectbox("Station", aq.STATIONS)
    day = st.date_input("Day")
    pm25 = st.number_input("PM2.5 (µg/m³)", min_value=0.0, max_value=500.0, value=0.0, step=0.5)
    sent = st.form_submit_button("Send report")
if sent:
    if pm25 <= 0:
        st.error("Enter the PM2.5 reading: it must be above zero.")
    else:
        aq.add_report(db, station, day, pm25)
        st.session_state.my_reports.append(station)
        st.success(f"Report saved for {station}.")
st.write(f"You've sent {len(st.session_state.my_reports)} report(s) this session.")

project.title: Build and deploy a data app
project.brief: A (fictional) city's environment team wants a public app where residents can explore air quality and send in their own readings, and you're building it. Start from the lab's explorer and air_quality.csv, or use a dataset of your own of a similar size (a few thousand rows at most), and build a multipage Streamlit app with st.navigation. It needs an overview page with KPI metrics and a trend chart; a detail page with a configured table, a second chart and a download; and a contribution page whose validated form stores entries in SQLite through a connection cached with st.cache_resource. Filters shared across pages live in session state, the data is cached with st.cache_data, and at least one part of a page is a fragment. Write at least six tests (pytest and AppTest), including one per page, and keep calculations in plain functions that are tested by import. Prepare it for deployment with a requirements.txt, a .streamlit/config.toml theme and any secrets read through st.secrets (nothing secret committed), then deploy it to Streamlit Community Cloud, or run it in Docker with the health check passing. Finish with a README that explains how to run, test and deploy it.
deliverables: The app's code: the entrypoint, the pages, a data module with the cached loaders, and the logic module
At least six passing tests, with the pytest output
requirements.txt, .streamlit/config.toml and a .gitignore that excludes secrets.toml and the database
A deployed app's address, or a Dockerfile and the output of docker ps showing the container healthy
A README: what the app does, how to run it, test it and deploy it, and which caches it uses and why

rubric.name: It works
rubric.description: Every page runs without errors; filters, the form and the download behave correctly, and missing input is handled with clear messages.

rubric.name: Layout and data display
rubric.description: Sidebar, columns and tabs organise the pages; charts and configured tables show the data clearly, with units.

rubric.name: Caching and performance
rubric.description: st.cache_data for data and st.cache_resource for the connection, used correctly; a fragment where it helps; no slow step repeated on every rerun.

rubric.name: State and forms
rubric.description: Shared filters in session state, callbacks used correctly, and a validated form that stores entries in the database.

rubric.name: Tests
rubric.description: At least six meaningful tests: logic tested by import and every page tested with AppTest, including widget interactions.

rubric.name: Deployment and configuration
rubric.description: Pinned requirements, a theme, secrets kept out of the repository, and a working deployment or a healthy container, with a clear README.
